Finite-mixture and latent-class count regression

Source: R/mixture_fit.R
countreg_mix.Rd

countreg_mix() estimates finite mixtures of count distributions and finite-mixture (latent-class) count regressions by maximum likelihood. countreg_lc() is the same model under the latent-class vocabulary (classes, membership_formula): both functions normalize their arguments into one specification and call one estimation engine, so equivalent calls give the same fit.

For unit \(u\) (a row, or a panel when group_var is given) the probability of the observed counts is $$L_u = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_{uk} \prod_{i \in u} f_k(y_i \mid x_i, \theta_k),$$ where \(f_k\) is the probability mass function of component \(k\) (any family of countreg(); see count_families) and \(\pi_{uk}\) are the mixing (class-membership) probabilities. The log-likelihood is \(\sum_u w_u \log L_u\), with frequency weights \(w_u\).

Usage

countreg_mix(
  formula,
  data,
  family = "POISSON",
  components = 2L,
  mixing_formula = ~1,
  fixed_mixing = NULL,
  shared = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_1 = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_2 = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  method = "BFGS",
  max.iters = 1000,
  start.vals = NULL,
  n_starts = 10L,
  seed = NULL,
  stderr = c("normal", "robust", "boot"),
  bootstraps = NULL,
  ndraws = 1500,
  engine = "quadrature",
  keep_data = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  control = mixture_control(),
  sp = NULL,
  rpar_formula = NULL,
  rpardists = NULL,
  correlated = FALSE,
  rpar_draws = 200
)

countreg_lc(
  formula,
  data,
  family = "POISSON",
  classes = 2L,
  membership_formula = ~1,
  fixed_mixing = NULL,
  shared = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_1 = NULL,
  dis_param_formula_2 = NULL,
  offset = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  group_var = NULL,
  method = "BFGS",
  max.iters = 1000,
  start.vals = NULL,
  n_starts = 10L,
  seed = NULL,
  stderr = c("normal", "robust", "boot"),
  bootstraps = NULL,
  ndraws = 1500,
  engine = "quadrature",
  keep_data = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  control = lc_control(),
  sp = NULL,
  rpar_formula = NULL,
  rpardists = NULL,
  correlated = FALSE,
  rpar_draws = 200
)

Arguments

formula

a model formula for the counts, as in countreg(). Use y ~ 1 for a mixture of distributions without covariates. Offsets can be given with offset() or the offset argument; the same offset applies to every component.

data

a data frame.

family

a family code (see count_families) used by every component, or one code per component (e.g. c(base = "POISSON", tail = "NB2")): a jointly estimated mixture of different families. Names become display labels of the components.

components, classes

the number of components (classes) \(K\). When family has several entries, it can be omitted.

mixing_formula, membership_formula

a one-sided formula for the mixing (class-membership) probabilities, a multinomial logit with the last component as reference: ~ 1 (default) gives constant proportions, ~ z lets them depend on z (a mixture of experts). For panel models, its variables must be constant within each panel.

fixed_mixing

optional known mixing probabilities (one per component, nonnegative, summing to 1). They are not estimated and add no parameters. These are not frequency weights or starting values. Zero probabilities are not allowed (the component would be unidentified).

shared

optional list saying which parameters are the same in all components: mean, a character vector of formula terms (use "(Intercept)" for the intercept; a factor is shared as a whole term), and dis1, dis2 (TRUE/FALSE) for the blocks of the first and second distribution parameter. Distribution parameters can only be shared between components of the same family. By default nothing is shared.

dis_param_formula_1, dis_param_formula_2

optional one-sided formulas for the first and second distribution parameter of the components, as in countreg(). They apply to every component whose family has the parameter (coefficients are component-specific unless shared).

offset, weights

an offset (column names, log scale) and frequency weights, as in countreg(). With group_var, weights must be constant within each panel: a weight stands for that many independent copies of the panel.

group_var

optional column name(s) identifying panels. All rows of a panel belong to the same (unknown) component, so the panel, not the row, is the independent unit; rows are independent given the component.

method

optimizer for the direct maximization of the observed log-likelihood (see countreg()); default "BFGS".

max.iters

maximum number of iterations of the direct maximization.

start.vals

optional starting values: a vector with one value per parameter (named as in coef(), or in that order). It is used as the first start; the others are generated.

n_starts

number of starts. Starts are reproducible from seed and are recorded in the fitted object (fit$model$starts).

seed

optional random seed for the generated starts (and the bootstrap). The caller's random-number stream is not changed. When NULL, a seed is drawn from the current stream and stored.

stderr

"normal" (from the Hessian of the observed-data log-likelihood), "robust" (sandwich with unit-level scores) or "boot" (nonparametric bootstrap of units, refitting the full mixture with several starts and aligning component labels).

bootstraps

number of bootstrap replicates for stderr = "boot" (default 200).

ndraws, engine

numerical settings of the mixed-Poisson families (PLN, PGE, PW, PLL) within each component, as in countreg(). They are unrelated to the number of components.

keep_data

logical; store the training data in the fitted object.

verbose

logical; report the progress of each start.

control

a mixture_control() object.

sp

optional fixed smoothing parameters for smooth terms (s(), te(), ...) in the formulas. Smooth terms may enter the mean, the distribution-parameter formulas and the mixing (membership) formula. Each component's copy of a smooth (and each membership logit's) has its own smoothing parameter; a smooth in a shared mean term is penalized once. The search over starts is unpenalized; the selected solution is then refitted by penalized likelihood with the smoothing parameters selected as in countreg(). Standard errors are Bayesian by default; the bootstrap is not available with smooths.

rpar_formula

optional one-sided formula of random parameters within the components (classes): ~ x makes the coefficient of x random, ~ 1 (or ~ 1 + x) the intercept as well (an implicit intercept does not count). The variables must also be in formula: each component's coefficient of a random variable is the mean of its random parameter (the location, for lognormal parameters), so the classes differ in the means of the random parameters, and also in their scales (Component<k>:SD:<variable>) unless shared = list(rpar = TRUE) gives all classes the same scales (Shared:SD:<variable>). See "Random parameters within classes" below.

rpardists

distributions of the random parameters, as in countreg_rp(): "n" (normal, the default), "ln", "t", "u" or "g", by name or one value for all.

correlated

TRUE for correlated (normal) random parameters, with a Cholesky factor (Chol:) in each class.

rpar_draws

the number of simulation draws of the random parameters for each unit (randomly shifted Halton points, a separate block for each unit, the same draws for every class up to the signs described in "Random parameters within classes"). They are generated from a seed derived from seed.

Value

An object of class c("countreg_mix", "flexCountReg") (countreg_mix()) or c("countreg_lc", "countreg_mix", "flexCountReg") (countreg_lc()). The methods coef(), vcov(), logLik(), AIC(), BIC(), summary(), predict() (predict.countreg_mix()), fitted(), residuals(), simulate(), tidy(), glance() and augment() work as for other models, and component_probs() returns prior or posterior class probabilities. rootogram(), cureplot() and margEffTable() (delta-method standard errors) accept mixture models.

Details

Estimation

Each start is a response-based or random preliminary partition of the units, turned into parameters by one M-step. Starts are improved by the EM algorithm (posterior class probabilities in the E-step; weighted updates of the component and mixing parameters in the M-step, with shared parameters updated jointly), and the best distinct solutions are polished by maximizing the observed-data log-likelihood directly with maxLik. The selected solution is the best polished one that converged. The start table (fit$model$starts) records every start's strategy, log-likelihood, EM iterations and status, and whether the best solution was reached by several starts; mixtures often have several local maxima, so a solution found by one start only deserves caution.

Components of the same family are exchangeable: their numbering is arbitrary. After estimation they are numbered in increasing order of their average expected count over the training rows (a display convention). Mixtures of different families keep the order given in family.

Parameters

The coefficients are named Component<k>:Mean:<term>, Component<k>:<parameter> (e.g. Component2:ln(alpha)), Shared:... for shared parameters, and Mixing:Component<k>:<term> for the membership logit of component \(k\) against the last component. Component expected counts use each family's own mean (for PLN and PLL it includes the lognormal factor), so shared link-scale coefficients do not imply equal component means.

Inference and model choice

The covariance matrix is the inverse of the observed information of the whole free parameter vector (not of the separate M-steps). Near a boundary (an almost empty component, or two almost identical components) it is unreliable; use the bootstrap and the start table. The usual chi-square likelihood-ratio test does not apply to comparing numbers of components (K versus K + 1); compare such models with AIC/BIC on the same sample, start stability and held-out log scores. regCompTest() refuses mixture models for this reason.

Random parameters within classes

With rpar_formula, the coefficients of some variables also vary within each class, from unit to unit (a latent-class random-parameters model). For unit \(u\) (a panel with group_var, otherwise a row), $$L_u = \sum_k \pi_{uk} \int \prod_{i \in u} f_k(y_i \mid x_i, \beta_k + b)\, dF_k(b),$$ with \(F_k\) the distribution of the random deviations in class \(k\): mean zero, and the class's scales. The latent classes capture discrete groups of units, and the random parameters the continuous variation within each. The integral is simulated with rpar_draws draws per unit, with analytic gradients through the posterior weights of the draws. Each start runs at most 25 EM iterations (EM converges slowly here) before the direct maximization finishes it. Every class uses the same draws of a unit (common random numbers): the class likelihoods stay unbiased, their simulation errors largely cancel in the posterior class probabilities, and relabeling the classes leaves the simulated likelihood unchanged. Different units have independent draws.

Only the absolute values of the scales are identified (and, with correlated = TRUE, the signs of the columns of each class's Cholesky factor): the fit reports positive standard deviations and a positive Cholesky diagonal. A Cholesky column is re-signed together with that class's standardized draws of the parameter (fit$model$rpar$signs), which leaves the simulated likelihood unchanged, so the reported maximum, gradient, Hessian and posterior probabilities all refer to the reported coefficients. Bootstrap refits are normalized the same way before their classes are aligned.

Predictions and probabilities integrate over the random parameters (predict(), component_probs(), rootogram(), residuals); simulate() draws new coefficients for every unit. The component expected counts are exact, from the moment generating functions of the random parameters (as method = "Exact" in countreg_rp()), when the family's mean is proportional to \(\mu\); they are Inf, with a warning, where the expected count does not exist (a lognormal random parameter with a positive variable, or a gamma one with \(x \sigma^2 / \mu \ge 1\)), and component variances likewise where the second moment does not exist. Count probabilities and class posteriors are simulated. Conditioning on outcomes ("posterior", "history") updates the class probabilities only, not the random parameters within the classes. Smooth terms are not yet available with random parameters.

Random parameters and classes can both explain heterogeneity, so the fit can be weakly identified: a class can stand in for a tail of a random parameter, and a large scale for a missing class. Shared scales (shared = list(rpar = TRUE)) are the more stable choice; compare the models with AIC/BIC and check the start table.

Interpretation

Classes are a modeling device. A good fit with two components does not show that two real subpopulations exist; the same mixture can describe a skewed or heavy-tailed distribution.

Zero-inflated, hurdle and underreporting components, component-specific formulas, and confidence/prediction/tolerance intervals for mixture predictions are not available yet.

References

McLachlan, G. J., & Peel, D. (2000). Finite Mixture Models. Wiley.

Grün, B., & Leisch, F. (2008). FlexMix version 2: Finite mixtures with concomitant variables and varying and constant parameters. Journal of Statistical Software, 28(4), 1-35.

Wedel, M., DeSarbo, W. S., Bult, J. R., & Ramaswamy, V. (1993). A latent class Poisson regression model for heterogeneous count data. Journal of Applied Econometrics, 8(4), 397-411.

See also

mixture_control(), component_probs(), predict.countreg_mix(), count_families

Examples

# A two-component Poisson mixture of simulated counts
set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(y = c(rpois(300, 1), rpois(200, 6)))
m <- countreg_mix(y ~ 1, data = d, family = "POISSON", components = 2,
                  n_starts = 5, seed = 42)
summary(m)
#> Call:
#> countreg_mix(formula = y ~ 1, data = d, family = "POISSON", components = 2, 
#>     n_starts = 5, seed = 42)
#> 
#> Finite-mixture count model with 2 components
#>   Component 1: POISSON
#>   Component 2: POISSON
#> Mixing: constant proportions (reference: Component 2)
#> Optimizer: BFGS + Newton-Raphson refinement | gradient close to zero (gradtol) 
#> 
#> Coefficients (standard errors: observed information (Hessian)):
#> 
#> Component 1 (POISSON):
#>                             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
#> Component1:Mean:(Intercept)  -0.0361     0.0828   -0.44     0.66
#> 
#> Component 2 (POISSON):
#>                             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> Component2:Mean:(Intercept)   1.8054     0.0374    48.2   <2e-16 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Mixing (multinomial logit):
#>                               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> Mixing:Component1:(Intercept)    0.407      0.117    3.49  0.00048 ***
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Component sizes:
#>       label  family  prior posterior effective_n modal_n mean_count
#>  Component1 POISSON 0.6003    0.6003       300.2     325     0.9646
#>  Component2 POISSON 0.3997    0.3997       199.8     175     6.0830
#> (prior: mean membership probability; posterior: mean posterior probability;
#>  effective_n: sum of posterior probabilities; modal_n: units whose most
#>  probable component it is; mean_count: average expected count)
#> 
#> Log-likelihood: -1107.547 | AIC: 2221.094 | BIC: 2233.738 | ICL: 2398.952 
#> N: 500
#> Entropy: 82.607 | relative entropy: 0.762 
#> Starts: 5 | 5 reached the selected log-likelihood
#> Observed information: positive definite (condition number 14.7 ) | max |gradient|: 4.82e-08 
#> No likelihood-ratio test of the number of components is reported (non-standard distribution).
component_probs(m, conditioning = "prior")[1, ]
#> Component1 Component2 
#>   0.600347   0.399653 

# \donttest{
# The same model through the latent-class interface
lc <- countreg_lc(y ~ 1, data = d, family = "POISSON", classes = 2,
                  n_starts = 5, seed = 42)
all.equal(logLik(m), logLik(lc))
#> [1] TRUE

# Latent-class NB2 regression with a membership covariate
data("abalone_rings")
fit <- countreg_lc(rings ~ shell_weight, data = abalone_rings,
                   family = "NB2", classes = 2,
                   membership_formula = ~ sex, n_starts = 5, seed = 1)
summary(fit)
